newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Norilsk sale takes place at crossroads.
newsitem.headline: Russian Norilsk sale takes place at crossroads.

text.p: The sale of Russia's Norilsk Nickel metals group, the newest powerhouse company to hit the auction blocks, represents the last of a dying breed in Moscow's crisis-ridden but fast-changing privatisation programme.
The Norilsk shares up for acquisition are the final stake available from one of the most controversial chapters in Russia's troubled property sell-off, a scheme known as shares-for-loans.

But the Norilsk auction is also taking place at a turning point in Moscow's privatisation programme, in which the government has recognised the need to raise the market value its companies can command and not just sell companies for a song.
"One chapter is ending just as another is beginning," said James Fenkner, head of research at CentreInvest consultancy, speaking of the timing and terms of the Norilsk sale.

There has been one story about the way in which sales of stakes originally acquired under shares-for-loans, long over, have been held -- the winners have been either the company holding the shares or an affiliated firm, making the deals seem pre-arranged.
"Will the cycle be broken with Norilsk?," asked a Western economist in London. "It would be a big surprise if it were."

That means the group offering the 38 percent Norilsk stake, powerful commercial bank Uneximbank, will probably win the auction, despite attacks from media controlled by powerful Russian banks and tycoons which recently lost an auction for another company won by an Uneximbank-led international group.
But the Norilsk stake will not come cheaply to Uneximbank.

The 38 percent stake, which represents 51 percent of voting shares, carries a starting price of around $487 million, covering stock, required investments and corporate debt relief. Bidding closes on Friday, with results due August 5.
Many say Uneximbank may be backed by cash from Western investment banks keen for a piece of one of the world's leading, albeit troubled, producers of nickel and precious metals.

Interfax news agency quoted Uneximbank's head, Vladimir Potanin, a former cabinet official, as saying the bank would be silly not to bid for its own stake after pumping so much cash and advice into financially-troubled Norilsk.
"It's hard to imagine a serious bidder other than Uneximbank," said Norilsk Nickel spokesman Sergei Vetchinin.
If Uneximbank wins what is effectively its own sale, it will do so despite being in the thick of the deepest trauma to hit Russia's financial and political circles in recent months.

Uneximbank earned the wrath of other powerful Russian banks when it teamed with U.S. financier George Soros and Western investment banks last week to win a quarter stake in Svyazinvest, placing a $1.875 billion bid in Russia's largest single sale.

The sale has sparked a crisis between the reformist cabinet -- which wanted to raise as much money as possible from the sale -- and media interests controlled by Russian groups which placed a losing bid for the company.
Russia's privatisation minister Alfred Kokh was quoted by Interfax as saying on Thursday the Norilsk sale would not pass without a row.
Uneximbank is carrying out a major restructuring programme at Norilsk, a mining and smelting powerhouse in the Arctic with major cost-cutting needs.
The only other company which has said publicly it is interested in Norilsk, Britain's Trans-World Group, says it has been shut out of bidding.

Under the shares-for-loans stage of privatisation, influential domestic banks and financial groups acquired the right to manage temporarily giant stakes in Russia's best companies in exchange for loans to the government.
The cash-strapped government has chosen not to repay the loans, letting the groups managing the stakes now offer them up through auctions.

Shares-for-loans, begun in 1995, represented the state's desperate need for immediate cash at bargain-basement prices, while the Svyazinvest sale shows Moscow wants the major money some of Russia's best companies are worth.

Norilsk is a hybrid of both elements, since the seller of the shares is almost certain to acquire them, but at a price which analysts say at least approaches reasonable market value. --Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
